answer:
KERNEL is the BGL Component to look at first. It has the most FATAL-level Log Entries of any Component, and they show up in every month of the log. Most of them come from one burst in June 2005, though, so the monthly count is falling. APP comes second: every one of its Log Entries is FATAL-level.

## Observed Facts
Data Scope: BGL Dataset, all dates, no message filter unless stated otherwise.

1. **KERNEL has the most FATAL-level Log Entries.**
   - It has 626,450 FATAL-level Log Entries [E3], out of 855,195 FATAL-level Log Entries across all Components [E3].
   - It also has the most Log Entries overall: 4,324,651 of 4,747,963 [E1]. Most of the dataset is INFO-level (3,735,813 Log Entries [E2]), so size alone doesn't show risk.
   - The most common alert tags all start with KERN: KERNDTLB 152,734, KERNSTOR 63,491, KERNMNTF 31,531, KERNTERM 23,338 Log Entries [E4].
   - Monthly KERNEL FATAL-level counts [E6]:

     | Month | Log Entries |
     |---|---|
     | Jun 2005 | 535,054 |
     | Jul 2005 | 9,393 |
     | Aug 2005 | 22,479 |
     | Sep 2005 | 28,909 |
     | Oct 2005 | 6,244 |
     | Nov 2005 | 15,109 |
     | Dec 2005 | 8,785 |
     | Jan 2006 | 477 |

2. **APP comes second.** All 228,536 of its Log Entries are FATAL-level [E1][E3]. The most common APP alert tag is APPSEV, with 49,651 Log Entries [E4].
3. **Smaller signals:**
   - MONITOR has 1,665 FAILURE-level Log Entries and BGLMASTER has 49 [E5].
   - LINKCARD has 206 FATAL-level Log Entries [E3].

## Hypotheses
- Most of the KERNEL FATAL count probably comes from one or a few events in June 2005, not a constant load. Even so, KERNEL keeps producing thousands of FATAL-level Log Entries a month after that, so it is a recurring problem rather than a one-off.
- The KERNDTLB and KERNSTOR tags suggest memory or storage faults on compute nodes. I haven't checked this against the message text.
- APP may be failing as a result of KERNEL faults rather than on its own. I haven't checked whether their timing lines up.

## Unknowns
- **Business impact:** The logs can't show financial loss, downtime, or customer or user impact.
- **Number of incidents:** These are Log Entry counts, not incidents. One fault can produce thousands of lines.
- **Spread across nodes:** I haven't checked how many nodes the KERNEL FATAL-level Log Entries come from, or whether one bad node drives most of them.
- **Cause of the June 2005 jump:** The cause isn't established.
- **Trend after January 2006:** The logs end in January 2006, so the trend after that can't be measured.

## Next Step
Count KERNEL FATAL-level Log Entries by node (`count_by` grouped by node) for June 2005 and for July 2005 to January 2006. This shows whether the risk is spread across the machine or comes from a few nodes. If it's a few nodes, replacing or isolating them is a cheap first step. Then run the same check for APP.
